title: What is known about 1RB0LF_1LC1RF_---1LD_0LE0LB_0RA0LA_0RA1RB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LF_1LC1RF_---1LD_0LE0LB_0RA0LA_0RA1RB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: The question is open. Lean proves only the generated bounded runs (no halt in 107 steps). Computed: no halt in the first 1010 steps; between resets the tape is a list of digits following one exact rule (282 of 289 transitions), and the resets, where the digits are rewritten, grow so fast that the seventh one, started at step 9,477,912, is still running at step 1010.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tmrun runs 1010 steps without a halt. D visits the left end of the tape 290 times, the last at step 9,477,912; each time the tape is a list of digits made of the words 0 1 1 and 0 0 1 1.

claims.title: The simple phase
claims.text: In 282 of the 289 transitions between left-end visits, a digit 2 is inserted after the first digit and the last digit loses 1: [1, d2, …, dk, n+1] → [1, 2, d2, …, dk, n]. The other seven are the first visit and six resets, which start when the last digit is 1 and last 202, 838, 12,278, 42,214, 580,526 and 6,080,814 steps.

claims.title: A reset longer than 10<sup>10</sup> steps
claims.text: The seventh reset starts from a 278-digit tape at step 9,477,912 and has not ended by step 1010; during it the tape is rewritten into other words (0 1 0 1^4 repeated), an inner counter not yet described.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.69×10<sup>15</sup> steps of an accelerated run
claims.text: Observed, not proved: the accelerated simulator rsim.py ran 1.69×1015 steps from blank tape without reaching a halting transition. Its tape, state and head position were equal to those of a plain C simulator at 6 checkpoints, the last at 1.13×1010 steps. Of these steps, the part after the last checkpoint rests on the simulator alone, including 2,254 trip-level jumps: a jump applies many identical round trips at once after seeing the same tape shape recur with constant count changes, which is validated against direct simulation but not proved.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Open. It halts exactly when B reads a 0 with a 0 on its left (0 B>0, then C reads 0). Deciding it needs a description of the resets.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows yet. Most of the time this machine keeps its tape as a list of digits and changes it in the simplest way: each round trip of the head puts a new digit 2 at the front and takes one off the last digit. When the last digit runs out, a long sweep rewrites everything, and these rewrites grow explosively: the seventh one has been running for more than 10<sup>10</sup> steps.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator.
Transitions between left-end visits that follow the simple digit rule.
The only way to halt: B reads a 0 with a 0 on its left.
No halt in the accelerated simulator (observed, not proved; checked against direct simulation up to 1.13×10<sup>10</sup> steps).

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.466).
After 109 steps the tape spans 59,010 cells (299 left of the start, 40,331 right), with a density of 1s of 0.668.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: What the tape is made of
html: Each time the head comes back to the left end in state D, the tape is made of two words, 0 1 1 and 0 0 1 1. Read every 0 0 1 1 as the start of a new digit and every 0 1 1 after it as one more; the tape is then a list of digits, such as [1, 225, 4, 4, 10, 10, 40, 28, 1] at step 98,599.

sections.heading: Resets that grow explosively
html: When the last digit is down to 1, a long sweep rewrites the list instead. The 2s at the front become 4s, and the digits behind them are recombined into new ones: [1, 225, 42, 102, 40, 28, 1] becomes [1, 426, 10, 84, 82, 153]. The resets took 202, 838, 12,278, 42,214, 580,526 and 6,080,814 steps; the next one, from a list of 278 digits, has been running since step 9,477,912 and was still running at 1010. During it the tape is written in yet other words, so a counter of its own is at work.

sections.heading: Where it could halt
html: The halting transition is C reading 0, and C is entered only when B reads a 0 and steps left. So the machine stops exactly when B meets a 0 with a 0 on its left. In 1010 steps that never happened.

sections.heading: What is proved
html: Lean: the halting configurations and no halt in 107 steps (generated). Computed: no halt in 1010 steps, and the digit rule above. Open: what a reset does, and the decision.

family: digit list with a simple phase and fast-growing resets
summary: Between long reorganising sweeps the tape is a list of digits in which each round trip inserts a 2 at the front and takes 1 off the last digit; the reorganising sweeps grow fast and the seventh one has run past 10<sup>10</sup> steps; no halt so far.
